Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Multi-omics Reveals Divergent Endothelial Molecular Responses to New and Old World Hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause vascular leakage syndromes that vary in clinical manifestation and severity. Although tissue tropism contributes to these differences, both Old and New World hantaviruses infect endothelial cells, where species-specific disease phenotypes remain poorly understood. Here we integrated time-resolved global RNA sequencing, mass spectrometry proteomics, and phosphoproteomics of human endothelial cells infected with New World Andes virus (ANDV) or Old World Hantaan virus (HTNV). Despite equivalent early viral RNA and protein levels, ANDV elicited a stronger innate immune protein response, preceding its restriction while HTNV replication continued. At later stages of infection, HTNV induced downregulation of cytoskeletal and junctional protein phosphorylation, accompanied by visual disruption of cellular actin architecture. Additionally, ANDV induced heightened activity of ERBB-family kinases, whose chemical inhibition by neratinib and afatinib reduced viral replication. Together, these data define species-specific responses in endothelial cells, identify druggable host targets, and reveal mechanisms with relevance to divergent vascular leakage symptomology.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause vascular leakage syndromes with variable clinical severity, and both Old and New World hantaviruses infect endothelial cells, yet species‑specific disease phenotypes remain poorly understood.
analysis.methods: Time‑resolved global RNA sequencing, mass‑spectrometry proteomics, and phosphoproteomics were performed on human endothelial cells infected with New World Andes virus (ANDV) or Old World Hantaan virus (HTNV).
analysis.results: Early infection showed equivalent viral RNA and protein levels, but ANDV elicited a stronger innate immune protein response preceding its restriction, whereas HTNV replication continued; later HTNV down‑regulated cytoskeletal and junctional protein phosphorylation with visible actin disruption; ANDV induced heightened ERBB‑family kinase activity, and inhibition with neratinib or afatinib reduced viral replication.
analysis.contribution: The study defines species‑specific endothelial responses, identifies druggable host kinase targets, and reveals mechanisms relevant to divergent vascular leakage symptomology.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is provided; detailed methods, sample sizes, and in‑vivo validation are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause vascular leakage syndromes of varying severity, and both Old and New World strains infect endothelial cells but species‑specific mechanisms are unclear. Methods: Time‑resolved RNA‑seq, proteomics and phosphoproteomics were applied to human endothelial cells infected with Andes virus (ANDV) or Hantaan virus (HTNV). Results: Early infection showed comparable viral RNA/protein levels, yet ANDV triggered a stronger innate immune protein response leading to restriction, while HTNV replication persisted; later HTNV down‑regulated cytoskeletal and junctional protein phosphorylation with actin disruption, and ANDV activated ERBB‑family kinases whose inhibition (neratinib, afatinib) reduced replication. Contribution: The work delineates species‑specific endothelial responses, identifies druggable host targets, and offers mechanistic insight into divergent vascular leakage. Limitations: Only abstract data are available; detailed experimental parameters and in‑vivo relevance are not reported.

papers.title_zh: 多组学揭示新世界和旧世界汉坦病毒的内皮分子反应差异

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒导致血管渗漏综合征,临床严重程度可变,且新旧世界的汉坦病毒均可感染内皮细胞,但物种特异的疾病表型仍了解不足。
analysis_zh.methods: 在感染新世界安第斯病毒(ANDV)或旧世界汉滩病毒(HTNV)的人类内皮细胞上进行时间分辨的全局RNA测序、质谱蛋白质组学和磷酸化蛋白质组学分析。
analysis_zh.results: 早期感染时病毒RNA和蛋白水平相当,但ANDV诱导更强的先天免疫蛋白响应并随后受到限制,而HTNV复制持续进行;随后HTNV下调细胞骨架和连接蛋白的磷酸化,伴随可见的肌动蛋白破坏;ANDV则激活ERBB家族激酶活性,使用neratinib或afatinib抑制可降低病毒复制。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究阐明了物种特异的内皮反应,识别出可药理干预的宿主激酶靶点,并揭示了与不同血管渗漏症状相关的机制。

papers.title: Molecular Surveillance and Evolutionary Characterization of Orthohantavirus jejuense in the Republic of Korea, 2019–2025
papers.abstract: Jeju virus (JJUV), a shrew-borne member of Orthohantavirus jejuense, has been detected in geographically separated populations of Crocidura shantungensis in the Republic of Korea (ROK). However, its distribution and evolutionary characteristics remain incompletely defined. From 2019 to 2025, 56 C. shantungensis were collected from 20 sites across the ROK and screened for JJUV RNA. Viral genomic sequences were characterized using next-generation and Sanger sequencing, followed by phylogenetic, evolutionary, selection-pressure, and in silico B-cell epitope analyses. JJUV RNA was detected in 7 of 56 shrews (12.5%) from Gwangju Metropolitan City, Cheorwon, Chuncheon, and Seogwipo. Coding-complete sequences of all three genomic segments were obtained from three variants, including two from Gwangju, providing genome-resolved evidence of JJUV circulation in the southern mainland. Phylogenetic analyses revealed clear geographic clustering of O. jejuense variants from the northern mainland, Gwangju, Jeju Island, and Ulleung Island. Estimated evolutionary rates ranged from 3.53 × 10−4 to 13.49 × 10−4 substitutions/site/year. Low ratios of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rates across the nucleocapsid protein, glycoproteins Gn and Gc, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase indicated predominantly purifying selection. Sequence- and structure-based analyses predicted six conserved linear B-cell epitope candidates across O. jejuense. Among these, Y165–K175 in the nucleocapsid protein showed the strongest combined structural support. These findings expand the known geographic and genomic diversity of O. jejuense and provide a framework for continued surveillance and future serological studies of its potential zoonotic relevance.
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

analysis.background: Jeju virus (JJUV), a shrew‑borne Orthohantavirus jejuense, has been detected in geographically separated populations of Crocidura shantungensis in the Republic of Korea, but its distribution and evolutionary characteristics remain incompletely defined.
analysis.methods: From 2019–2025, 56 C. shantungensis were collected from 20 sites across the ROK and screened for JJUV RNA (A3, A4). Positive samples underwent next‑generation and Sanger sequencing, followed by phylogenetic, evolutionary, selection‑pressure, and in silico B‑cell epitope analyses (A5).
analysis.results: JJUV RNA was detected in 7 of 56 shrews (12.5%) from four locations (A6). Coding‑complete sequences of all three genome segments were obtained from three variants, including two from Gwangju (A7). Phylogenetic analysis showed clear geographic clustering of variants from the northern mainland, Gwangju, Jeju Island, and Ulleung Island (A8, A9). Estimated evolutionary rates ranged 3.53 × 10⁻⁴–13.49 × 10⁻⁴ substitutions/site/year (A10). Low dN/dS ratios across N, Gn, Gc, and RdRp indicated predominant purifying selection (A11). In silico analyses identified six conserved linear B‑cell epitopes, with Y165–K175 in the nucleocapsid protein receiving the strongest structural support (A12, A13).
analysis.contribution: These findings expand the known geographic and genomic diversity of O. jejuense and provide a framework for continued surveillance and future serological studies of its potential zoonotic relevance.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available, so detailed methods, sample‑size justification, and statistical analyses are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Jeju virus (JJUV), a shrew‑borne Orthohantavirus jejuense, has been detected in geographically separated Crocidura shantungensis populations in Korea, but its distribution and evolution are incompletely defined. Methods: From 2019–2025, 56 shrews from 20 sites were screened for JJUV RNA; positives were sequenced by NGS and Sanger and analyzed phylogenetically, evolutionarily, for selection pressure, and for B‑cell epitopes. Results: JJUV RNA was found in 7/56 shrews (12.5%) across four locations; complete genomes from three variants (two from Gwangju) showed geographic clustering, evolutionary rates of 3.53‑13.49 × 10⁻⁴ subs/site/yr, purifying selection, and six conserved B‑cell epitopes, notably Y165‑K175. Contribution: The work broadens known geographic/genomic diversity of O. jejuense and offers a surveillance and serology framework. Limitations: Only an abstract is provided, lacking detailed methodological and statistical information.

papers.title_zh: 2019–2025年大韩民国正汉坦病毒 jejuense的分子监测与进化特征表征

analysis_zh.background: Jeju病毒(JJUV),一种携带于鼩鼱的 正汉坦病毒 jejuense,已在大韩民国分布于不同地区的山东鼩鼱(Crocidura shantungensis)群体中检测到,但其分布范围和进化特征仍未完全阐明。
analysis_zh.methods: 2019至2025年间,在大韩民国的20个地点采集了56只C. shantungensis,并对其进行JJUV RNA筛查(A3,A4)。阳性样本随后进行下一代测序和Sanger测序,并开展系统发育、进化、选择压力及体外B细胞表位分析(A5)。
analysis_zh.results: 在四个地点的56只鼩鼱中检测到7只(12.5%)携带JJUV RNA(A6)。从三种变体中获得了全部三个基因组片段的完整编码序列,其中两株来自光州(A7)。系统发育分析显示,来自北部大陆、光州、济州岛和乌陵岛的变体呈明显的地理聚类(A8,A9)。估计的进化速率为3.53 × 10−4–13.49 × 10−4 替代/位点/年(A10)。N、Gn、Gc和RdRp基因的dN/dS比值均偏低,表明以净化选择为主(A11)。体外分析鉴定出六个保守的线性B细胞表位,其中核衣壳蛋白的Y165–K175表位获得最强的结构支持(A12,A13)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些发现扩展了已知的O. jejuense的地理和基因组多样性,并为持续监测及其潜在人畜共患相关性的未来血清学研究提供了框架。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,未报告详细方法、样本量依据及统计分析。

papers.title: Habitat-Mediated Spillover Risk of Andes Hantavirus in Oligoryzomys longicaudatus: A Mechanistic Eco-Epidemiological Model
papers.abstract: Andes hantavirus (ANDV) is a rodent-borne orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in southern South America. Its maintenance and spillover risk depend on the ecology of its principal reservoir, Oligoryzomys longicaudatus, and on environmental changes that alter habitat availability, host abundance, and human–rodent interfaces. We developed a mechanistic eco-epidemiological model that couples effective habitat cover to an SIR framework for ANDV transmission in O. longicaudatus. Habitat degradation and compensatory restoration modify rodent carrying capacity, natality, and the force of infection, which depends on infected host load relative to instantaneous ecological capacity. We derived the habitat equilibrium, the basic reproduction number R0, and the time-dependent effective reproduction number Re(t) and evaluated infection-burden and threshold indicators across degradation-restoration scenarios. The analysis shows that R0 is independent of equilibrium habitat cover because susceptible abundance scales with carrying capacity at the disease-free equilibrium. In contrast, Re(t), cumulative incidence, and infected load depend on transient habitat-mediated crowding. Restoration increases reservoir abundance and absolute infection burden, whereas degradation can reduce abundance while increasing crowding-driven transmission pressure and prolonging supercritical windows. These results identify ecological conditions under which habitat change may intensify reservoir infection pressure and guide One Health surveillance at human–rodent interfaces.

papers.title_zh: 栖息地介导的安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒 在长尾鼠 Oligoryzomys longicaudatus 中的溢出风险:机制性生态流行病学模型

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒 汉坦病毒(ANDV)是一种啮齿动物传播的 正汉坦病毒,在南美洲南部导致 汉坦病毒心肺综合征,其溢出风险取决于主要宿主长尾鼠 Oligoryzomys longicaudatus 的生态学。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者构建了一个机制性生态流行病学模型,将有效栖息地覆盖率与 ANDV 在 O. longicaudatus 中传播的 SIR 框架耦合。
analysis_zh.results: 模型显示基本再生数 R0 与平衡栖息地覆盖率无关,因为易感个体数量随容纳量成比例增长;然而,时变有效再生数 Re(t)、累计发病率和感染负荷受瞬时栖息地导致的拥挤影响;栖息地恢复增加宿主数量和绝对感染负担,而退化虽可降低数量,却会提升拥挤驱动的传播压力并延长超临界窗口。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些结果明确了栖息地变化可能加剧宿主感染压力的生态条件,并为人畜接口的 One Health 监测提供指导。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供了摘要;未报告详细数据、参数取值及模型验证。

papers.full_text: Letters to the Editor 1 Research Letter Hantavirus Infection as a Mimic of Rheumatic Disease: A Selective Diagnostic Approach To the Editor: Recent public health alerts have renewed attention to hantavirus infection, an uncommon but potentially severe zoonosis.1,2 For rheumatologists, its relevance is selective but clinically important in compatible contexts. Hantavirus infection may initially present as an acute febrile inflammatory syndrome with arthritis, arthralgia, or myalgia, variably accompanied by thrombocytopenia, endothelial dysfunction, and renal or pulmonary involvement.3 In patients referred for suspected rheumatic disease, this constellation of signs and symptoms may overlap with inflammatory arthritis, systemic autoimmune disease, immune-mediated renal disease, or vasculitis. The central issue is a diagnostic one: Hantavirus may behave as an infectious mimic of rheumatic disease while the diagnostic evaluation is still ongoing, and treatment decisions may have substantial consequences. Hantavirus should not be considered on the basis of isolated fever or musculoskeletal symptoms alone. Rather, it should enter the rheumatology differential when fever and musculoskeletal manifestations occur together with thrombocytopenia and renal, urinary, pulmonary, capillary leak, or hemorrhagic features, especially when epidemiologic exposure is compatible. Clinically, this phenotype may resemble selected rheumatic presentations, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)–associated vasculitis, antiglomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease, adult-onset Still disease, inflammatory myopathy, infection-triggered arthritis, or undifferentiated systemic autoimmune disease. Relevant exposures include contact with rodents or rodent-contaminated environments, occupational or domestic exposure in rural or peridomestic settings, recent travel to endemic areas, or exposure associated with an epidemiologically linked hantavirus cluster.3 The epidemiologic pattern is geographically structured. Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is encountered mainly across Europe and Asia, whereas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is recognized chiefly in the Americas, with the distribution of individual orthohantaviruses determined by the ecology of their reservoir hosts.3 To date, limited ­ person-to-person transmission has been documented only for Andes virus, a hantavirus endemic to South America.3 The published literature, although limited, illustrates several diagnostic challenges relevant to rheumatology. Musculoskeletal involvement is usually nonspecific; arthralgia and myalgia may accompany HFRS and, in some adults, may be sufficiently prominent to resemble an early inflammatory presentation.4 Thrombocytopenia, renal dysfunction, proteinuria, hema- turia, and hypocomplementemia may prompt consideration of systemic autoimmune or immune-mediated renal disease, including SLE, vasculitis, immune-mediated nephritis, and anti-GBM disease, thereby increasing the risk of diagnostic misclassification. Hantavirus-induced acute kidney injury may mimic immune-mediated glomerular disease, including anti-GBM disease or lupus nephritis, before serologic confirma- tion clarifies the diagnosis.5,6 Vasculitis-like presentations require particular caution. A recent report described myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA– positive pauci-immune small vessel vasculitis with progressive renal dysfunction during acute hantavirus infection.7 This obser- vation establishes a temporal and clinical association but does not demonstrate causation. Earlier serologic data also argue against a frequent relationship. Among 191 patients with estab- lished systemic vasculitides, including granulomatosis with poly- angiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and giant cell arteritis, no hantavirus-specific antibodies were detected.8 These findings therefore support diag- nostic vigilance rather than a causal interpretation, particularly when infection-related organ injury and primary autoimmune vasculitis share clinical, serological, or histopathological features. SARS-CoV-2 infection may offer a useful clinical reference for rheumatologists when considering the interface between viral infection and rheumatic disease. Both SARS-CoV-2 and hantaviruses are RNA viruses capable of eliciting prominent systemic inflammatory responses and, in selected cases, arthritis or vasculitis-like manifestations that may resemble ­ immune-mediated disease.3,9,10 Experience with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has heightened awareness that viral infections may both mimic and intersect with rheumatic phenotypes. Hantavirus infection may be viewed within this same diagnostic framework, although the underlying biology and clinical syndromes are distinct. full_text_sections.full_text: Letters to the Editor 1 Research Letter Hantavirus Infection as a Mimic of Rheumatic Disease: A Selective Diagnostic Approach To the Editor: Recent public health alerts have renewed attention to hantavirus infection, an uncommon but potentially severe zoonosis.1,2 For rheumatologists, its relevance is selective but clinically important in compatible contexts. Hantavirus infection may initially present as an acute febrile inflammatory syndrome with arthritis, arthralgia, or myalgia, variably accompanied by thrombocytopenia, endothelial dysfunction, and renal or pulmonary involvement.3 In patients referred for suspected rheumatic disease, this constellation of signs and symptoms may overlap with inflammatory arthritis, systemic autoimmune disease, immune-mediated renal disease, or vasculitis. The central issue is a diagnostic one: Hantavirus may behave as an infectious mimic of rheumatic disease while the diagnostic evaluation is still ongoing, and treatment decisions may have substantial consequences. Hantavirus should not be considered on the basis of isolated fever or musculoskeletal symptoms alone. Rather, it should enter the rheumatology differential when fever and musculoskeletal manifestations occur together with thrombocytopenia and renal, urinary, pulmonary, capillary leak, or hemorrhagic features, especially when epidemiologic exposure is compatible. Clinically, this phenotype may resemble selected rheumatic presentations, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)–associated vasculitis, antiglomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease, adult-onset Still disease, inflammatory myopathy, infection-triggered arthritis, or undifferentiated systemic autoimmune disease. Relevant exposures include contact with rodents or rodent-contaminated environments, occupational or domestic exposure in rural or peridomestic settings, recent travel to endemic areas, or exposure associated with an epidemiologically linked hantavirus cluster.3 The epidemiologic pattern is geographically structured. Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is encountered mainly across Europe and Asia, whereas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is recognized chiefly in the Americas, with the distribution of individual orthohantaviruses determined by the ecology of their reservoir hosts.3 To date, limited ­ person-to-person transmission has been documented only for Andes virus, a hantavirus endemic to South America.3 The published literature, although limited, illustrates several diagnostic challenges relevant to rheumatology. Musculoskeletal involvement is usually nonspecific; arthralgia and myalgia may accompany HFRS and, in some adults, may be sufficiently prominent to resemble an early inflammatory presentation.4 Thrombocytopenia, renal dysfunction, proteinuria, hema- turia, and hypocomplementemia may prompt consideration of systemic autoimmune or immune-mediated renal disease, including SLE, vasculitis, immune-mediated nephritis, and anti-GBM disease, thereby increasing the risk of diagnostic misclassification. Hantavirus-induced acute kidney injury may mimic immune-mediated glomerular disease, including anti-GBM disease or lupus nephritis, before serologic confirma- tion clarifies the diagnosis.5,6 Vasculitis-like presentations require particular caution. A recent report described myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA– positive pauci-immune small vessel vasculitis with progressive renal dysfunction during acute hantavirus infection.7 This obser- vation establishes a temporal and clinical association but does not demonstrate causation. Earlier serologic data also argue against a frequent relationship. Among 191 patients with estab- lished systemic vasculitides, including granulomatosis with poly- angiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and giant cell arteritis, no hantavirus-specific antibodies were detected.8 These findings therefore support diag- nostic vigilance rather than a causal interpretation, particularly when infection-related organ injury and primary autoimmune vasculitis share clinical, serological, or histopathological features. SARS-CoV-2 infection may offer a useful clinical reference for rheumatologists when considering the interface between viral infection and rheumatic disease. Both SARS-CoV-2 and hantaviruses are RNA viruses capable of eliciting prominent systemic inflammatory responses and, in selected cases, arthritis or vasculitis-like manifestations that may resemble ­ immune-mediated disease.3,9,10 Experience with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) has heightened awareness that viral infections may both mimic and intersect with rheumatic phenotypes. Hantavirus infection may be viewed within this same diagnostic framework, although the underlying biology and clinical syndromes are distinct. From a clinical perspective, severe hantavirus disease, particularly HCPS, may progress rapidly to fulminant cardiopulmonary failure, with case fatality rates reaching up to 50% in the Americas.2,3 Accordingly, hantavirus testing should be guided by the overall clinical and epidemiologic pattern rather than used routinely in rheumatology. Serologic testing may be appropriate when fever and musculoskeletal symptoms coexist with throm- bocytopenia, renal or pulmonary involvement, and a compatible exposure history; reverse transcription PCR can be considered in selected settings according to disease timing, severity, and local laboratory availability. Testing is most useful while the differen- tial diagnosis remains unresolved, particularly before substantial immunomodulatory treatment is initiated. The Figure summa- rizes this selective approach. The central practical implication is selective case recognition rather than routine screening. During periods of increased hanta- virus activity or recognized outbreaks, testing should be reserved for patients in whom the clinical phenotype and exposure history are concordant. Such an approach may reduce premature diagnostic closure, help distinguish infection-related endothelial The Journal of Rheumatology 2026;xx:xxxx doi:10.3899/jrheum.2026-0485 First Release September 15 2026 © 2026 The Journal of Rheumatology 2 The Journal of Rheumatology injury from primary rheumatic disease, and support more accu- rate classification of acute febrile inflammatory presentations. In selected cases, distinguishing infection-related inflammatory presentations, including hantavirus-associated disease, from primary rheumatic disease may also affect the timing or appro- priateness of immunomodulatory therapy. Methods: not reported in the supplied evidence. Results: not reported in the supplied evidence. Contribution: The authors suggest a selective testing strategy—serology or PCR only when the clinical phenotype and exposure history align—to avoid misdiagnosis and inappropriate immunomodulation (F23,F25,F26). papers.full_text: nature health News ‘Desperate rodents’ pose hantavirus risk to humans — boosted by climate change and deforestation Rapid urbanization and changes in rodent behaviour increase the risk of human disease outbreaks, especially in Africa, but experts fear surveillance gaps leave most zoonotic infections undetected. By Tsitsi Bhobo W hen the Andes hantavirus cir­ culated on the M/V Hondius cruise ship, South Africa’s specialist hospitals quickly admitted infected patients and sequenced the virus. But infectious dis­ ease scientists warn that locally derived hanta­ virus strains — including the lethal Sangassou virus — are circulating undetected, hosted by native shrews, rodents and bats1. “At the moment, we believe that hanta­ virus probably is more prevalent [and] widespread than diagnosed in Africa,” says Tulio de Oliveira, Professor at Stellenbosch University, South Africa, and director of the Centre for Epidemic Response and Innova­ tion. Such infections are mainly “self-limited transmission clusters between rodents, other animals and humans,” he tells Nature Health. De Oliveira’s lab is one of a small number across Africa that test for viruses in wild animals, including rodents, bats and non- human primates. Surveillance gap Hantaviruses pose a bigger systematic dan­ ger to Africa’s public health architecture than previously thought, argued de Oliveira and colleagues in a recent article. Limited diag­ nostic and testing capacity and lack of moni­ toring infrastructure, combined with climate change and urbanization, are leading to more zoonotic outbreaks. Africa has a clinical surveillance gap, with viral spillovers probably occurring without being detected by stretched public health authorities. During the current Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda, many of the early infections were suspected to be cases of malaria, leading to delays in the public health response. The DRC has the second highest bur­ den of malaria in the world, leading to tens of thousands of deaths each year. Many other zoonotic infections could be missed. Hillary Young, an ecologist at the University of California Santa Barbara, USA, notes that “we don’t know how big the burden of hanta­ virus is because we haven’t looked for it, really. We don’t have that surveillance.” “One of the acute problems facing Africa is that there is little clinical research into the ecology of hantaviruses, [such as] which specific animals host them,” she says. Such research, including genetics, would “empower scientists to map the interaction between hosts and viruses and calculate the possible harm to humans — in real time,” she adds. With surveillance capacity absent, doctors often report possible hantavirus infections as ‘fever of unknown origin’. “It’s hard, because hantavirus is another one of these diseases that kind of overlaps with lots of other unex­ plained febrile diseases,” says Young. This challenge persists despite South Africa having amongst the best infectious disease genomic surveillance infrastructure in the world. Laboratories across Africa are usually focused on supporting clinical studies in humans, but during outbreaks, resources are diverted to test animals for zoonotic infec­ tions. There are only a small number of such labs across the continent, such as the South Africa National Institute for Communicable Diseases, the Institut Pasteur de Dakar in Senegal and the Uganda Virus Research Unit. These labs act very quickly to develop reagents for new pathogens, test samples and develop metagenomics assays, but the bottleneck leads to inevitable delays, with zoonotic out­ breaks often underdiagnosed for weeks. Urbanization and deforestation Hantavirus spillover in Africa is likely to be linked to loss of biodiversity, rapid urbaniza­ tion and climate change. A recent outbreak of hantaviruses in South America spread beyond rural settings and into urban environments, Hantavirus particles under an electron microscope, with colour enhanced. CREDIT: ALFRED PASIEKA/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/GETTY nature health News possibly because climate variations are lead­ ing to milder and shorter winters in Argentina. Rapid urbanization — widespread across the continent — leads to increased risk, as rats breed in cities where residents regularly interact with wildlife. “We’ll have a bigger pro­ liferation of concentrated rodents,” in Africa’s fast-urbanizing landscapes, says Young, lead­ ing to more zoonotic outbreaks. Young’s research has shown how declines in large wildlife in East Africa were associated with an increase in the prevalence of a rodent- borne bacterium, Bartonella, which can infect humans — providing a link between biodiver­ sity loss and zoonotic disease outbreaks2. Climate change and change of land use in Africa drive rodents to find new breeding zones in human landscapes, warns Young. Rapid expansion of cities across Africa, many without investment in sewerage, creates food and opportunities for rodent species that are already adapted to live alongside humans. This creates the conditions for ‘boom dynamics’, says Young, where rodent popula­ tions increase rapidly. This means periods of explosive, exponential growth for rat popula­ tions followed by often calamitous declines3. “You might get really desperate rodents,” she says, where the animals are “forced into kind of aggressive behaviour. Fighting in rodents can help spread disease among them at higher prevalence.” One Health The genomic surveillance labs in Africa, Latin America and Asia have considerable expertise but fewer resources than their counterparts in high-income countries, says Young. Despite these constraints, they are doing valuable work closest to the regions where zoonotic diseases are most likely to spring up. Africa is taking a lead in shifting the ‘One Health’ model towards building long-term skills, surveillance and diagnostics infrastructure in the global south, the type of capacity that remains resilient through crises. Several African countries, including the DRC and Uganda, have adopted ‘One Health’ frame­ works, an approach pioneered by Rwanda4. But such frameworks need to extend beyond the countryside and integrate with cities in Africa, rather than thinking of these urban spaces as separated from wild rural environ­ ments, says Young. De Oliveira stresses that, although hanta­ viruses are unlikely to cause large human outbreaks — because of the biology of the virus — funding cuts for global health pose challenges. There is now a “big lack of global health funding,” he says, with the US and many Euro­ pean countries “running out of money for global health because of other priorities such as defence”. During the current Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda, many of the early infections were suspected to be cases of malaria, leading to delays in the public health response. The DRC has the second highest bur­ den of malaria in the world, leading to tens of thousands of deaths each year. Many other zoonotic infections could be missed. Hillary Young, an ecologist at the University of California Santa Barbara, USA, notes that “we don’t know how big the burden of hanta­ virus is because we haven’t looked for it, really. We don’t have that surveillance.” “One of the acute problems facing Africa is that there is little clinical research into the ecology of hantaviruses, [such as] which specific animals host them,” she says. Such research, including genetics, would “empower scientists to map the interaction between hosts and viruses and calculate the possible harm to humans — in real time,” she adds. With surveillance capacity absent, doctors often report possible hantavirus infections as ‘fever of unknown origin’. “It’s hard, because hantavirus is another one of these diseases that kind of overlaps with lots of other unex­ plained febrile diseases,” says Young. This challenge persists despite South Africa having amongst the best infectious disease genomic surveillance infrastructure in the world. Laboratories across Africa are usually focused on supporting clinical studies in humans, but during outbreaks, resources are diverted to test animals for zoonotic infec­ tions. There are only a small number of such labs across the continent, such as the South Africa National Institute for Communicable Diseases, the Institut Pasteur de Dakar in Senegal and the Uganda Virus Research Unit. These labs act very quickly to develop reagents for new pathogens, test samples and develop metagenomics assays, but the bottleneck leads to inevitable delays, with zoonotic out­ breaks often underdiagnosed for weeks. Urbanization and deforestation Hantavirus spillover in Africa is likely to be linked to loss of biodiversity, rapid urbaniza­ tion and climate change. A recent outbreak of hantaviruses in South America spread beyond rural settings and into urban environments, Hantavirus particles under an electron microscope, with colour enhanced. CREDIT: ALFRED PASIEKA/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/GETTY nature health News possibly because climate variations are lead­ ing to milder and shorter winters in Argentina. Rapid urbanization — widespread across the continent — leads to increased risk, as rats breed in cities where residents regularly interact with wildlife. “We’ll have a bigger pro­ liferation of concentrated rodents,” in Africa’s fast-urbanizing landscapes, says Young, lead­ ing to more zoonotic outbreaks. Young’s research has shown how declines in large wildlife in East Africa were associated with an increase in the prevalence of a rodent- borne bacterium, Bartonella, which can infect humans — providing a link between biodiver­ sity loss and zoonotic disease outbreaks2. Climate change and change of land use in Africa drive rodents to find new breeding zones in human landscapes, warns Young. Rapid expansion of cities across Africa, many without investment in sewerage, creates food and opportunities for rodent species that are already adapted to live alongside humans. This creates the conditions for ‘boom dynamics’, says Young, where rodent popula­ tions increase rapidly. This means periods of explosive, exponential growth for rat popula­ tions followed by often calamitous declines3. “You might get really desperate rodents,” she says, where the animals are “forced into kind of aggressive behaviour. Fighting in rodents can help spread disease among them at higher prevalence.” One Health The genomic surveillance labs in Africa, Latin America and Asia have considerable expertise but fewer resources than their counterparts in high-income countries, says Young. Despite these constraints, they are doing valuable work closest to the regions where zoonotic diseases are most likely to spring up. Africa is taking a lead in shifting the ‘One Health’ model towards building long-term skills, surveillance and diagnostics infrastructure in the global south, the type of capacity that remains resilient through crises. Several African countries, including the DRC and Uganda, have adopted ‘One Health’ frame­ works, an approach pioneered by Rwanda4. But such frameworks need to extend beyond the countryside and integrate with cities in Africa, rather than thinking of these urban spaces as separated from wild rural environ­ ments, says Young. De Oliveira stresses that, although hanta­ viruses are unlikely to cause large human outbreaks — because of the biology of the virus — funding cuts for global health pose challenges. There is now a “big lack of global health funding,” he says, with the US and many Euro­ pean countries “running out of money for global health because of other priorities such as defence”. papers.title: Hantavirus: biology, immune responses, and pathogenesis
papers.abstract: Abstract The recent Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise has raised global public health alarms due to its dangerous ability to person-to-person spread. Hantavirus infections primarily manifest as hemorrhagic fever with Eurasian renal syndrome (HFRS) and Americas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), both characterized by endothelial manifestation. Two principal mechanisms, virus-mediated cytopathy and host-driven immunopathology, have been proposed to account for the pathological progression, while their interplay is yet to be fully explored. In this review, we synthesize the recent research on hantavirus biology, cellular entry mechanisms, and epidemiological characteristics, and particularly highlight that viral immune evasion and subsequent uncontrolled host immune responses act as the core pathogenic drivers. Hantaviruses employ diverse strategies to antagonize type I interferon signaling and autophagy, which delay early innate immune activation and enable extensive viral dissemination. The excessive activation of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, combined with functionally impaired regulatory T cells and dysregulated humoral immunity, initiates severe inflammatory cascades, which in turn disrupt endothelial barrier integrity and cause organ vasculopathy. We also outline current therapeutic and preventive strategies, along with key directions for future research. A better understanding of hantavirus immunopathogenesis will help develop improved countermeasures against this zoonotic disease.

papers.full_text: Cell Death and Disease REVIEW ARTICLE | Article in Press Hantavirus: biology, immune responses, and pathogenesis Yufang Shi ●Mauro Piacentini ●Alimuddin Zumla ●Yu Wang ●Qing Li ●Ying Wang ● Jun Zhou ●Gerry Melino ●Giuseppe Ippolito Received: 13 June 2026 / Revised: 3 August 2026 / Accepted: 25 August 2026 © The Author(s) 2026 Abstract The recent Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise has raised global public health alarms due to its dangerous ability to person-to-person spread. Hantavirus infections primarily manifest as hemorrhagic fever with Eurasian renal syndrome (HFRS) and Americas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), both characterized by endothelial manifestation. Two principal mechanisms, virus-mediated cytopathy and host-driven immunopathol- ogy, have been proposed to account for the pathological progression, while their interplay is yet to be fully explored. In this review, we synthesize the recent research on hantavirus biology, cellular entry mechanisms, and epidemiological characteristics, and particularly highlight that viral immune evasion and subsequent uncontrolled host immune responses act as the core pathogenic drivers. Hantaviruses employ diverse strategies to antagonize type I interferon signaling and autophagy, which delay early innate immune activation and enable extensive viral dissemination. The excessive activation of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, combined with functionally impaired regulatory T cells and dysregulated humoral immunity, initiates severe inflammatory cascades, which in turn disrupt endothelial barrier integrity and cause organ vasculopathy. We also outline current therapeutic and preventive strategies, along with key directions for future research. A better understanding of hantavirus immunopathogenesis will help develop improved countermeasures against this zoonotic disease. Facts ●Paradox of Hantavirus Pathogenesis: Based on current epidemiological and clinical evidence, this review highlights the central paradox of host–pathogen interactions, wherein hantaviruses cause severe immunopathology in humans while maintaining asymptomatic persistent infections in rodent reservoirs. ●Shift to an Immunopathogenic Framework: To better elucidate the mechanisms of vascular breakdown, this review proposes a transition from a virus-centric model to an immune-mediated framework, systematically integrating early viral IFN-I evasion, excessive CD8+ T cell/NK cell activation, and Treg deficiency. ●Therapeutic Potential and Research Priorities: While targeted immunomodulators and novel single-dose mRNA vaccines show promise in mitigating severe disease, precise mapping of the receptor-tropism-pathogenesis axis, immune calibration kinetics, and host tolerance mechanisms remains critical for future clinical interventions This Article in Press is shared early to give you faster access to new research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. The final edited version will replace it automatically. Cell Death and Disease https://doi.org/10.1038/s41419-026-09235-6 Introduction: the central paradox of hantavirus pathogenesis Hantaviruses present a classic paradigm in emerging infectious disease biology, where the central mechanistic puzzle remains fundamentally unresolved: how does a pathogen that establishes persistent, asymptomatic infection in its natural rodent reservoirs trigger severe, frequently lethal immunopathology upon spillover into accidental human hosts [1]? This biological dichotomy sits at the critical intersection of viral molecular biology, host-endothelial dynamics, and immunopathogenesis—domains that have generated competing explanatory frameworks over four decades of research [1, 2]. The two clinically distinct manifestations—hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and han- tavirus cardiopulmonary/pulmonary syndrome (HCPS/HPS) in the Americas—share an underlying mechanism of endothelial barrier disruption, yet diverge in target organ tropism and severity profiles [1, 2]. The field has oscillated between two dominant explanatory paradigms: a virus-centric model emphasizing direct cytopathic effects and a host-centric model foregrounding immune-mediated vascular damage. Contemporary evi- dence increasingly favors a synthesis in which viral immune evasion strategies paradoxically amplify subsequent immunopathology, but the precise mechanistic architecture of this interplay remains contested [3–5]. The urgency of resolving these contested mechanistic details has been underscored by an atypical, high-profile outbreak in May 2026 aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius [6]. This cluster, rapidly traced to Andes virus (ANDV) infection, has renewed focus on the unique biological features of New World hantaviruses—particularly their capacity for person-to-person transmission within closed environments [6, 7]. Fig. 1 Structural characteristics of hantavirus and its key proteins. A Schematic representation of the Orthohantavirus Andesense virion structure and genome organization. (Adapted and modified from https://viralzone.expasy.org/11847). B Structure of hantavirus envelope glycoprotein Gc in postfusion conformation in presence of 600 mM KCL (PDB: 5LJX). C High-resolution in situ ANDV single tetramer structure (PDB: 9P3I). D CryoEM structure of Hantavirus ANDV Gn(H) protein complex with 2Fabs ANDV-5 and ANDV-34 (PDB: 8DBZ). Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41419-026-09235-6 Cell Death and Disease Table 1 Evolutionary distribution, geographic reservoir segregation, and target organ disease phenotypes of major pathogenic hantaviruses. Viral Species Lineage Primary Natural Reservoir Host Vector Family Taxonomy Geographic Distribution \Primary Human Clinical Manifestation Target Organ Vulnerability Hantaan virus (HTNV) Apodemus agrarius (Striped field mouse) Muridae Eurasia Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) Renal Glomerular Microvasculature Puumala virus (PUUV) Myodes glareolus (Bank vole) Cricetidae Europe Nephropathia Epidemica (Mild HFRS) Renal Tubules & Epithelial Junctions Sin Nombre virus (SNV) Peromyscus maniculatus (Deer mouse) Cricetidae North America Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS/HCPS) Pulmonary Endothelium & Alveoli Andes virus (ANDV) Oligoryzomys longicaudatus (Long- tailed colilargo) Cricetidae South America Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS/HCPS) Systemic Vasculature & Airway Monolayers Long-term co-speciation within distinct small mammal families ensures persistent, non-lytic asymptomatic carriage in specific hosts. Accidental exposure of the human vascular network to aerosolized excreta from these specific reservoirs determines whether pathology shifts toward Eurasia-centric renal damage or Americas-centric cardiopulmonary syndrome. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41419-026-09235-6 Article in Press Cell Death and Disease Here, we synthesize the current scientific literature to map the evolving research landscape on hantaviruses across six key interconnected domains: viral biology and molecular structure, mechanisms of cellular entry and infection, innate and adaptive immune responses, pathogenic mechanisms of vascular leakage, global epidemiological trends, and emerging therapeutic and prophylactic strategies. Viral biology: molecular architecture and evolutionary constraints Genomic organization and structural determinants Hantaviruses are enveloped negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses within the Hantaviridae family of the order Bunyavirales [4, 8, 9]. The genome contains three segments: the large (L) segment for RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), the medium (M) segment for glycoprotein precursor (GPC, cleaved co-translationally into envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc), and the small (S) segment for nucleocapsid protein (NP)(Fig.1A). This tripartite segmented architecture permits genetic reassortment, conferring evolutionary flexibility that may generate viral variants with novel pathogenic properties [10]. The glycoproteins Gn and Gc are critical determinants of host cell tropism and are the primary targets for neutralizing antibody responses (Figs. 1B – D) [11, 12]. The M segment thus occupies a central position in pathogenicity determination: it encodes the molecules responsible for cellular attachment, membrane fusion, and the principal neutralization epitopes. Point mutations in glycoprotein sequences can profoundly alter viral infectivity, as demonstrated by studies showing that two amino acid substitutions in Old World hantavirus glycoproteins are sufficient to generate highly infectious recombinant vectors [13]. The evolutionary stability of these segments is illustrated by real-time genomic sequencing from the May 2026 MV Hondius outbreak cluster. Genomic sequencing and characterisation complemented the epidemiological investigation into the point of origin and subsequent transmission [14]. Each of the S, M, and L genomic segments from the three hantavirus isolates displays high sequence consistency. This observation suggests that the virus has not undergone reassortment, an evolutionary event in which segmented viral strains swap genetic fragments to generate new variants. Accordingly, the virus linked to this outbreak most probably originates from a single genetically stable lineage, instead of arising from recent genetic recombination between distinct hantavirus strains [14]. The RdRp and cap-snatching mechanism The L segment-encoded RdRp mediates both transcription and replication. A distinctive feature of hantavirus mRNA synthesis is the cap-snatching mechanism, whereby the viral RdRp cleaves short capped RNA primers from mRNAs of host origin to initiate viral transcription. This process requires host cell factors, establishing a fundamental dependency on the cellular transcriptional machinery [15]. This host factor requirement for cap snatching represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability, as disruption of this interaction could selectively inhibit viral replication without directly targeting host processes. Host reservoir biology and spillover dynamics Each hantavirus species has co-evolved with a specific rodent host reservoir in which persistent, asymptomatic infection is maintained (Table 1) [16]. The striped field mouse (Apodemus agrarius) serves as the main natural reservoir host of Hantaan virus (HTNV). In European regions, bank voles (Myodes glareolus) act as persistent carriers that preserve Puumala virus (PUUV) [16]. The ANDV virus is carried by Oligoryzomys longicaudatus, a wild rodent commonly called the long-tailed colilargo. The geographical range of this species extends from northern Chile and northwestern Argentina where there is a stable population. This rodent is not naturally present in Europe and in the United States, and established wild Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s41419-026-09235-6 Cell Death and Disease populations of this species are completely absent abroad. This is crucial since introduction to local rodent populations and potential subsequent rodent-to-human transmission in Europe is not expected [16]. Human infection is accidental, occurring primarily through inhalation of aerosolized virus-containing rodent excreta (urine, feces, saliva) [4, 16]. The mechanisms by which reservoir hosts suppress pathology while maintaining viremia—likely involving regulatory T cell-mediated immunosuppression—stand in stark contrast to the hyperin- flammatory response in humans [3, 11]. Understanding this dichotomy remains one of the field’s central theoretical challenges. Sustained human-to-human transmission has been validated only for ANDV among hantavirus species [7, 17]. The outbreak on the MV Hondius is considered a case study of a potential superspreader scenario, allowing the effects of prolonged case contact, closed ventilation, delayed symptom appearance and late diagnosis to be studied in a real-life context. All conditions were present to allow secondary cases aboard the ship and tertiary cases across international borders [7]. Mechanisms of cellular entry and tropism Receptor utilization and endothelial tropism Hantaviruses preferentially target endothelial cells, which constitutes the mechanistic basis for the vascular pathology that defines both HFRS and HCPS [4]. The primary cellular receptors for pathogenic hantaviruses include αvβ3 integrin for pathogenic strains, and αvβ1 integrin for non-pathogenic strains, and latest work identifies PCDH1 as a key receptor governing the cellular entry of New World hantaviruses [18]. This receptor specificity provides a molecular explanation for endothelial tropism and suggests that the tropism itself—rather than any direct cytopathic mechanism—positions the virus to trigger vascular dysfunction through immune-mediated collateral damage (Fig. 2). Non-lytic infection and its pathogenic implications A critical distinguishing feature of hantavirus biology is that infection of endothelial cells is non-cytopathic [19]. Unlike many hemorrhagic fever viruses that destroy target cells directly, hantaviruses establish productive infection without inducing overt cellular damage. This non-lytic character has profound implications for pathogenesis theory: it necessarily redirects pathogenic mechanisms toward indirect, immune-mediated injury rather than direct viral cytopathology (Fig. 2). Furthermore, hantaviruses actively inhibit apoptosis in infected cells, promoting viral per- sistence and potentially amplifying subsequent immune-mediated damage when cytotoxic responses eventually target infected endothelium [20]. Infection is non-lytic, with viral inhibition of apoptosis promoting persistence. Pathogenesis arises from indirect, immune-mediated endothelial activation and vascular dysfunction, rather than direct cytopathology. (Created in https://BioRender.com). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41419-026-09235-6 Article in Press Cell Death and Disease Immune responses: the double-edged sword Hantavirus immunopathogenesis is driven by viral immune evasion and subsequent host immune dysregulation. Suppression of type I interferon signaling by the virus promotes systemic dissemination. Together with regulatory T cell deficiency and hyperactivation of CD8+ T cells, NK cells, and B cells, these cells elicit exaggerated cytotoxic responses, which ultimately cause endothelial damage, complement activation and vascular leakage in severe infections (Fig. 3). Innate immune activation and viral evasion Hantaviruses have evolved sophisticated mechanisms to evade and delay innate immune detection, particularly the type I interferon (IFN-I) response [21]. The IFN-I signaling pathway, mediated through RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs), is the primary cellular sensor for hantavirus RNA. However, multiple viral proteins actively antagonize this pathway: the glycoprotein cytoplasmic tail inhibits TRAF3/TBK1-directed IRF3 activation, while the nucleocapsid protein (NP) sequesters double-stranded RNA intermediates to prevent RLR activation [22]. Recent work has identified TRIM25 as a specific target of Hantaan virus immune evasion. HTNV inhibits the type I interferon response by targeting RLR signaling pathways through TRIM25 [21]. By disrupting normal autophagic signaling, these viral proteins suppress IFN-I production and inflammatory cytokine secretion, creating a permissive environment for early viral replication. The theoretical significance of these evasion strategies extends beyond mere immune escape. By delaying the initial innate response, hantaviruses allow greater viral dissemination before adaptive immunity is engaged. When the adaptive response finally mounts, it confronts a more widely distributed infection, necessitating a more vigorous effector response—one that, in the context of endothelial tropism, inevitably causes collateral vascular damage. This “delay-and-amplify” model represents the current leading framework for understanding hantavirus immunopatho- genesis [3, 5]. Mononuclear phagocyte redistribution A marked redistribution of peripheral mononuclear phagocytes (MNPs) to the airways occurs during acute Puumala virus (PUUV) infection, which likely drives localized immune activation at the initial infection focus [3]. Pathogenic hantaviruses can replicate within cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS), and this replication capacity has been proposed as a determinant of pathogenicity [24]. The ability to productively infect and disseminate through MPS cells may explain systemic viral spread and the multi-organ involvement characteristic of severe hantavirus disease. Cytotoxic lymphocyte responses: CD8+ T cells and NK cells The adaptive immune response to hantavirus infection is dominated by a vigorous cytotoxic lymphocyte response involving both CD8+ T and NK cells. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) studies in patients with acute PUUV infection have revealed increased numbers of activated CD8+ T and NK cells, along with elevated granzyme A and granzyme B [25]. Hantavirus infections primarily manifest as hemorrhagic fever with Eurasian renal syndrome (HFRS) and Americas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), both characterized by endothelial manifestation. Two principal mechanisms, virus-mediated cytopathy and host-driven immunopathol- ogy, have been proposed to account for the pathological progression, while their interplay is yet to be fully explored. In this review, we synthesize the recent research on hantavirus biology, cellular entry mechanisms, and epidemiological characteristics, and particularly highlight that viral immune evasion and subsequent uncontrolled host immune responses act as the core pathogenic drivers. Hantaviruses employ diverse strategies to antagonize type I interferon signaling and autophagy, which delay early innate immune activation and enable extensive viral dissemination. The excessive activation of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, combined with functionally impaired regulatory T cells and dysregulated humoral immunity, initiates severe inflammatory cascades, which in turn disrupt endothelial barrier integrity and cause organ vasculopathy. We also outline current therapeutic and preventive strategies, along with key directions for future research. A better understanding of hantavirus immunopathogenesis will help develop improved countermeasures against this zoonotic disease.
