KEYWORDS AI-generated medical images, Andes virus, artificial intelligence, hantavirus, misinformation, pandemic preparedness TYPE Perspective PUBLISHED 10 September 2026 DOI 10.3389/fdgth.2026.1887820 Frontiers in Digital Health 01 frontiersin.org Introduction Compared to the COVID-19 pandemic, the current information landscape is being profoundly reshaped by the widespread availability of generative artificial intelligence (genAI). Large language models (LLMs), multimodal AI systems, and generative image platforms are now increasingly integrated into healthcare communication, scientific dissemination, clinical documentation, and medical education (1). At the same time, concerns regarding the misuse of genAI in medicine are rapidly emerging. Recent literature has documented multiple real-world incidents involving AI-generated misinformation, hallucinated medical content, unsafe clinical suggestions, biased algorithmic outputs, and misleading patient-facing communication (2, 3). The growing accessibility of genAI tools means that highly realistic medical-looking content can now be produced by virtually anyone within minutes, including radiological images, histological slides, microbiological results, and clinical documentation (4–6). This results in “synthetic medical realism,” defined as multimodal AI-generated content that simulates authentic clinical, laboratory, or institutional medical materials. Unlike during the COVID-19 pandemic, when misinformation spread primarily through fabricated narratives, edited videos, screenshots, and decontextualized media (7), contemporary AI tools can generate synthetic medical artifacts that closely reproduce the visual language and institutional aesthetics of authentic healthcare documentation (8). The case On May 12, 2026, Italian media outlets reported the isolation and hospitalization at “Luigi Sacco Hospital” in Milan of a contact linked to a confirmed Andes virus (ANDV) case associated with the MV Hondius outbreak reported on May 4, 2026, by the World Health Organization (WHO) (9). One article included an image, disclosed as AI-generated, of a hand holding a document presented as a diagnostic report for ANDV, showing a “NEGATIVE” result (10) (Figure 1). The alleged hospital laboratory report reproduced the visual identity of “Luigi Sacco Hospital”, potentially increasing its perceived authenticity. Closer inspection revealed multiple inconsistencies, including inaccurate institutional branding, absence of patient identifiers, atypical microbiological terminology, and reporting features inconsistent with contemporary digitally validated laboratory workflows. The overall visual composition also reflected the hyper-realistic aesthetic typical of contemporary AI-generated images, designed to appear convincing during rapid consumption while remaining fragile under professional scrutiny. Further articles published during the same week by major Italian newspapers included AI-generated images depicting positive hantavirus tests, Italian authorities screening alleged hantavirus contacts at the airport, and hospital-based infectious disease response activities (11–13). In these last three examples the use of genAI for the creation of these realistic images has not been disclosed. These episodes may simply reflect an editorial decision to illustrate news articles using synthetic content. However, even when not intentionally deceptive, the circulation of realistic but non-authentic medical-looking documents, samples, and procedures may distort public risk perception, reinforce the impression of clinically verified information, and contribute to misunderstanding during infectious disease (ID) alerts when public attention is heightened. Discussion In recent weeks, increasing media attention regarding hantavirus infections has generated understandable public concern particularly on social media platforms and digital communication channels. Within this context, the online circulation of an alleged hospital laboratory report related to hantavirus testing, reproducing the visual identity of “Luigi Sacco Hospital” in Milan, which is a referral centre for ID and pandemic preparedness, represents an emblematic example of the new challenges introduced by AI-generated medical realism. The central issue may extend beyond the falsification of a single medical document. The broader concern is the emergence of “synthetic medical realism”: AI-generated content capable of exploiting the symbolic and visual authority traditionally associated with healthcare institutions. Medicine relies heavily on visual trust, and medical images are not only neutral representations of reality but also sociocultural constructions that shape credibility and transmit certainty (14). Laboratory reports, radiological images, pathology slides, and hospital- branded documents are frequently perceived as credible before undergoing verification. As a result, fabricated medical content presented in a convincing-enough medical form may rapidly activate cognitive trust mechanisms among patients, journalists, and even healthcare professionals. Recent literature increasingly supports these concerns. Zhu et al. demonstrated that ChatGPT integrated with image- generation tools could create convincing blood smears, Western blots, immunofluorescence images, and other experimental biomedical figures, raising substantial concerns regarding scientific integrity and medical misinformation (4). Similarly, Hartung et al. showed that even domain experts failed to reliably distinguish AI-generated histological images from authentic ones, highlighting the growing difficulty of identifying fabricated biomedical content (5). Tordjman et al. recently demonstrated that radiologists struggled to reliably distinguish synthetic radiographs generated by AI systems from authentic imaging studies (6). In their analysis, neither human experts nor AI detection systems consistently identified all deepfake radiological images. Together, these findings suggest that future ID outbreaks may unfold within a profoundly different communication environment compared with COVID-19. The next infodemic may not simply involve false information but highly realistic synthetic medical content capable of visually simulating clinical authenticity. This phenomenon may have important public-health implications, not limited to isolated episodes of misinformation, but rather including amplification of public anxiety during outbreaks, confusion regarding testing indications, inappropriate Colaneri et al. 10.3389/fdgth.2026.1887820 Frontiers in Digital Health 02 frontiersin.org utilization of resources, and erosion of trust in healthcare institutions. For example, synthetic representations of hospital diagnostic reports may incorrectly suggest that specialized ID testing is universally accessible or routinely indicated, potentially generating unrealistic public expectations and unnecessary pressure on healthcare services. The rapid adoption of genAI in medicine may be outpacing the development of adequate governance frameworks. Current regulatory systems may still be poorly equipped to address AI- generated hallucinations, synthetic medical images, pseudo- clinical outputs, and multimodal misinformation (15). The case described here is emblematic. Although the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (16), which requires disclosure of AI-generated or manipulated audiovisual content that could falsely appear authentic (“deepfakes”), represents an important regulatory step, the relevant transparency obligations under Article 50 will apply only from 2 August 2026, almost three months after the incident described here. Moreover, AI-generated medical content may rapidly circulate across jurisdictions and digital platforms beyond the direct scope of EU regulation and enforcement. The Digital Services Act (17) addresses a different regulatory layer by focusing primarily on intermediary services and online platforms rather than news publishers acting as editorial content producers. The incident therefore illustrates a transitional and functional regulatory gap: realistic AI-generated medical-looking content may circulate before the AI Act’s dedicated transparency obligations become applicable. Furthermore, recent analyses have emphasized that only a minority of AI-enabled medical tools have undergone rigorous interventional clinical evaluation before implementation, and many LLM-based systems used in healthcare communication fall outside traditional medical-device regulatory pathways (18, 19). FIGURE 1 AI-generated ANDV diagnostic report. AI-generated Virology report displaying a negative Hantavirus RNA screening result using Real-Time PCR analysis performed at the Microbiology lab of Ospedale Luigi Sacco, Milan, Italy. Reproduced with permission from “HANTAVIRUS: TURISTA NEGATIVO AL SACCO” by mi_tomorrow. Colaneri et al. 10.3389/fdgth.2026.1887820 Frontiers in Digital Health 03 frontiersin.org Several ethical concerns remain unresolved, including limited transparency regarding AI-generated outputs, unclear accountability for misinformation-related harm, propagation of algorithmic bias, and inappropriate delegation of medical authority to non-validated systems (20). AI-generated medical realism should be considered a potential emerging category of public health risk during ID emergencies. Therefore, traditional fact-checking approaches alone may prove insufficient in the near future, and public-health institutions, scientific journals, and healthcare providers may increasingly need to confront the challenge of synthetic medical realism. Future preparedness strategies may warrant coordinated action across multiple actor groups. Public health institutions should develop rapid institutional verification systems for suspicious medical content circulating during outbreaks, and establish public communication protocols that anticipate and addressing synthetic medical misinformation before it shapes public risk perception during ID alerts. News media outlets should adopt and enforce explicit editorial standards requiring clear disclosure of AI-generated imagery, particularly when such content depicts or resembles clinical documentation, hospital materials, or outbreak-related medical information as the absence of disclosure, even when unintentional, may distort public perception. Digital platforms should implement scalable monitoring systems capable of detecting and flagging AI- generated health misinformation during outbreak events, and invest in the development and integration of digital watermarking and content-authenticity verification tools to facilitate rapid identification of synthetic medical content. Scientific journals should establish explicit submission guidelines and editorial policies, while regulators could consider expediting the implementation and updating of European regulations on this matter in a sector-specific manner, to promptly close transitional regulatory gaps as illustrated by this case. In conclusion, the unregulated use of genAI may represent a significant emerging threat to public health communication during infectious disease emergencies, highlighting the urgent need for stronger policies focused on the education, regulation, and monitoring of AI-generated media as a key preparedness strategy. papers.full_text: Subjects Emerging infectious disease preparedness has traditionally focused on emergency medicine, infectious disease, and critical care specialists. However, the ophthalmologist is not insulated from emerging infectious disease. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak highlights why ophthalmologists should also be incorporated into outbreak surveillance and response. Throughout history, ophthalmologists have played an important role in identifying infectious diseases through their ocular manifestations. Yet, this role depends on a clear understanding of a pathogen’s ophthalmic phenotype. Despite growing attention surrounding the current Andes virus outbreak, the ocular manifestations of this pathogen remain largely undefined. This knowledge gap presents both an opportunity and a responsibility for ophthalmologists to systematically characterise ocular involvement and contribute to emerging infectious disease surveillance. Herein, we review the available evidence regarding ocular involvement in hantavirus infection and contend that ophthalmologists have a critical role in defining the ocular phenotype of Andes virus during the current outbreak. The Andes strain of Hantavirus was recently documented aboard an international vessel. In April 2026, passengers and crew aboard the MV Hondius, began developing severe respiratory illness during an itinerary across the South Atlantic. The World Health Organization was notified on May 2, 2026, and Andes virus was confirmed as the causative pathogen on May 5 [1]. As of late-May 2026, 13 confirmed or probable cases and 3 deaths had been reported across multiple countries, with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) monitoring several individuals across multiple US states [2]. Although the overall public health risk in the United States remains low, the CDC has issued a Health Alert Network advisory emphasising heightened clinical vigilance. Hantaviruses (family Hantaviridae) are enveloped, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA viruses transmitted primarily through aerosolisation of infected rodent excrement, causing two principal syndromes: hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) from New World hantaviruses including Sin Nombre and Andes viruses, and haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) from Old World hantaviruses such as Puumala, Hantaan, and Seoul viruses. Andes virus is the only hantavirus with recently confirmed person-to-person transmission, typically via respiratory secretions during prolonged close contact with a symptomatic individual [3]. The ophthalmic literature on hantavirus is dominated by Puumala virus, which causes nephropathia epidemica (NE), a generally mild to moderate, renal-predominant form of HFRS. In the largest prospective ophthalmic series to date, Hautala et al. examined 92 eyes of 46 serologically confirmed NE patients and found that 70% reported ocular symptoms during acute illness, with decreased IOP in 88%, reduced visual acuity in 87%, conjunctival chemosis in 87%, crystalline lens thickening in 82%, a myopic shift in 78%, anterior chamber shallowing in 64%, and shortened vitreous length in 52% [4]. All anterior segment changes resolved fully with systemic recovery. Transient myopia is the hallmark finding, occasionally exceeding −4.0 diopters [5]. External findings include periorbital oedema, conjunctival injection, and subconjunctival haemorrhage [4,5,6]. Posterior findings are less frequent but include retinal haemorrhages, macular oedema, retinal whitening near the optic disc, and a self-limiting posterior necrotising retinitis, with neuro-ophthalmic manifestations possible when CNS complications such as hypophyseal haemorrhage occur [5]. Although ocular manifestations of Puumala strain of hantavirus infection are well described, virtually no ophthalmic data exist for Andes virus, the pathogen responsible for the current outbreak. This distinction is critical because existing ophthalmic knowledge is derived from a different virus, a different clinical syndrome, and a substantially different severity spectrum. What we do know is that in contrast to the Puumala virus, the systemic manifestations of the Andes virus causes HPS, a fulminant cardiopulmonary illness in which patients progress rapidly to respiratory failure, mechanical ventilation, and in severe cases extracorporeal support [7]. To date, no ophthalmic evaluation of HPS patients has been published. This gap in knowledge has practical consequences. Clinically, this means that the pattern of presentation that ophthalmologists may be tasked to recognise is extrapolated from a population that differs in virus, syndrome severity, and clinical state. The existing literature on the Puumala virus may be used to prompt suspicion (i.e., a febrile patient with bilateral unexplained myopic shift should raise the possibility of hantavirus), but it cannot yet tell ophthalmologists what Andes virus ocular disease looks like beyond that. The current outbreak represents not only a clinical challenge but also a scientific opportunity. For ophthalmologists, this means that every HPS patient managed at a US referral centre during the current outbreak who is well enough to undergo ophthalmic evaluation represents an opportunity to generate evidence that does not yet exist. A standardised assessment, documented and reported in the literature, would begin to answer a question that the existing literature cannot. Importantly, ophthalmologists should examine patients with known or suspected hantavirus using correct transmission-based precautions. Unlike other hantaviruses, Andes virus has documented person-to-person transmission via respiratory secretions, a characteristic with no known analogue among other hantaviruses. For ophthalmologists, this distinction is particularly relevant because slit-lamp examination requires prolonged face-to-face proximity. Consequently, infection-control preparedness should be considered. The CDC recommends airborne infection isolation with gown, gloves, eye protection, and an N95 or higher-level respirator for any patient with confirmed or suspected infection [2]. Historically, ophthalmologists have contributed immensely to the recognition and characterisation of systemic infectious diseases through their ocular manifestations. From syphilis and tuberculosis to more recent outbreaks involving Zika virus, Mpox, and COVID-19, ocular findings have occasionally provided diagnostic clues, insight into disease pathogenesis, and opportunities for longitudinal monitoring. The Andes virus should be viewed within this broader framework. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak carries with it a powerful lesson. We as ophthalmologists are not peripheral observers during emerging infectious disease events. We contribute to surveillance, diagnosis, characterisation of novel ocular manifestations, and implementation of appropriate infection-control practices. As the outbreak evolves, systematic ophthalmic evaluation of affected patients may help close a major knowledge gap regarding the ocular manifestations of the Hantavirus Andes strain infection. Posterior findings are less frequent but include retinal haemorrhages, macular oedema, retinal whitening near the optic disc, and a self-limiting posterior necrotising retinitis, with neuro-ophthalmic manifestations possible when CNS complications such as hypophyseal haemorrhage occur [5]. Although ocular manifestations of Puumala strain of hantavirus infection are well described, virtually no ophthalmic data exist for Andes virus, the pathogen responsible for the current outbreak. This distinction is critical because existing ophthalmic knowledge is derived from a different virus, a different clinical syndrome, and a substantially different severity spectrum. What we do know is that in contrast to the Puumala virus, the systemic manifestations of the Andes virus causes HPS, a fulminant cardiopulmonary illness in which patients progress rapidly to respiratory failure, mechanical ventilation, and in severe cases extracorporeal support [7]. To date, no ophthalmic evaluation of HPS patients has been published. This gap in knowledge has practical consequences. Clinically, this means that the pattern of presentation that ophthalmologists may be tasked to recognise is extrapolated from a population that differs in virus, syndrome severity, and clinical state. The existing literature on the Puumala virus may be used to prompt suspicion (i.e., a febrile patient with bilateral unexplained myopic shift should raise the possibility of hantavirus), but it cannot yet tell ophthalmologists what Andes virus ocular disease looks like beyond that. The current outbreak represents not only a clinical challenge but also a scientific opportunity. For ophthalmologists, this means that every HPS patient managed at a US referral centre during the current outbreak who is well enough to undergo ophthalmic evaluation represents an opportunity to generate evidence that does not yet exist. A standardised assessment, documented and reported in the literature, would begin to answer a question that the existing literature cannot. Importantly, ophthalmologists should examine patients with known or suspected hantavirus using correct transmission-based precautions. Unlike other hantaviruses, Andes virus has documented person-to-person transmission via respiratory secretions, a characteristic with no known analogue among other hantaviruses. For ophthalmologists, this distinction is particularly relevant because slit-lamp examination requires prolonged face-to-face proximity. Consequently, infection-control preparedness should be considered. The CDC recommends airborne infection isolation with gown, gloves, eye protection, and an N95 or higher-level respirator for any patient with confirmed or suspected infection [2]. Historically, ophthalmologists have contributed immensely to the recognition and characterisation of systemic infectious diseases through their ocular manifestations. From syphilis and tuberculosis to more recent outbreaks involving Zika virus, Mpox, and COVID-19, ocular findings have occasionally provided diagnostic clues, insight into disease pathogenesis, and opportunities for longitudinal monitoring. The Andes virus should be viewed within this broader framework. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak carries with it a powerful lesson. We as ophthalmologists are not peripheral observers during emerging infectious disease events. We contribute to surveillance, diagnosis, characterisation of novel ocular manifestations, and implementation of appropriate infection-control practices. As the outbreak evolves, systematic ophthalmic evaluation of affected patients may help close a major knowledge gap regarding the ocular manifestations of the Hantavirus Andes strain infection. papers.title: Toward medical countermeasures against hantaviruses.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are zoonotic threats that can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and severe cardiopulmonary syndrome. Despite disease severity, there are no approved vaccines or therapeutics available for the prevention or management of hantavirus infections. Here, we discuss advances in the development of vaccines, neutralizing antibodies, and small-molecule antiviral therapeutics.

papers.title: Admission-Time Clinicolaboratory Phenotypes for Early Differentiation of Severe Fever With Thrombocytopenia Syndrome and Hemorrhagic Fever With Renal Syndrome.
papers.abstract: Early differentiation of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains difficult in endemic settings. In this single-center retrospective comparative study, we analyzed admission-time demographic, clinical, and laboratory data from 330 hospitalized patients with laboratory-confirmed SFTS (n = 220) or HFRS (n = 110) admitted between May 2023 and November 2025. Compared with HFRS, SFTS showed an older age distribution, female predominance, more frequent neurological symptoms, and a predominantly hematologic phenotype with modest hepatic differences, whereas HFRS showed more prominent urinary manifestations and greater inflammatory and renal abnormalities. Abnormality-based and normalized organ-domain burden analyses supported the same phenotypic separation, with hematologic, renal, and inflammatory domains showing the clearest exploratory differences. Two differentiation models were developed as proof-of-concept tools using the same complete-case data set and internally evaluated by full-process nested cross-validation. The basic and extended models achieved out-of-fold AUCs of 0.975 and 0.971, respectively; the paired difference was -0.004 (95% CI, -0.014 to 0.005; p = 0.404). Adding CRP, albumin, and LDH did not provide consistent incremental predictive value. These single-center findings provide a proof-of-concept framework requiring independent external validation and recalibration before potential clinical application.

source_records.abstract: Early differentiation of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains difficult in endemic settings. In this single-center retrospective comparative study, we analyzed admission-time demographic, clinical, and laboratory data from 330 hospitalized patients with laboratory-confirmed SFTS (n = 220) or HFRS (n = 110) admitted between May 2023 and November 2025. Compared with HFRS, SFTS showed an older age distribution, female predominance, more frequent neurological symptoms, and a predominantly hematologic phenotype with modest hepatic differences, whereas HFRS showed more prominent urinary manifestations and greater inflammatory and renal abnormalities. Abnormality-based and normalized organ-domain burden analyses supported the same phenotypic separation, with hematologic, renal, and inflammatory domains showing the clearest exploratory differences. Two differentiation models were developed as proof-of-concept tools using the same complete-case data set and internally evaluated by full-process nested cross-validation. The basic and extended models achieved out-of-fold AUCs of 0.975 and 0.971, respectively; the paired difference was -0.004 (95% CI, -0.014 to 0.005; p = 0.404). Adding CRP, albumin, and LDH did not provide consistent incremental predictive value. These single-center findings provide a proof-of-concept framework requiring independent external validation and recalibration before potential clinical application.

analysis.background: Early differentiation of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains difficult in endemic settings (A1).
analysis.methods: A single‑center retrospective comparative study analyzed admission‑time demographic, clinical, and laboratory data from 330 hospitalized patients with laboratory‑confirmed SFTS (n=220) or HFRS (n=110) admitted May 2023–Nov 2025 (A2); two differentiation models were built on the complete‑case dataset and internally evaluated by full‑process nested cross‑validation (A5).
analysis.results: SFTS patients were older, more often female, and showed more neurological and hematologic abnormalities, whereas HFRS patients had more urinary, inflammatory, and renal abnormalities (A3); organ‑domain burden analyses confirmed these phenotypic separations (A4). The basic and extended models achieved out‑of‑fold AUCs of 0.975 and 0.971, respectively, with a paired difference of –0.004 (95% CI –0.014 to 0.005) (A6, A7); adding CRP, albumin, and LDH did not consistently improve prediction (A8).
analysis.contribution: The study provides a phenotypic framework and high‑performing proof‑of‑concept models for early SFTS vs HFRS differentiation, informing clinical triage and surveillance (A4, A5, A9).
analysis.limitations: Findings are from a single center, based on abstract‑only data, and require independent external validation and recalibration before clinical application (A9).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Early differentiation of SFTS and HFRS is difficult in endemic areas. Methods: A single‑center retrospective comparative study analyzed admission‑time demographic, clinical, and laboratory data from 330 hospitalized patients with laboratory‑confirmed SFTS (n=220) or HFRS (n=110) between May 2023 and November 2025; two predictive models were built using complete‑case data and evaluated by nested cross‑validation. Results: SFTS patients were older, more often female, and showed more neurological and hematologic abnormalities, whereas HFRS patients had more urinary, inflammatory, and renal abnormalities; organ‑domain analyses confirmed these separations. The basic and extended models achieved AUCs of 0.975 and 0.971, with a non‑significant paired difference of –0.004 (95% CI –0.014 to 0.005); adding CRP, albumin, and LDH gave no consistent improvement. Contribution: Provides a phenotypic framework and high‑performing proof‑of‑concept models for early SFTS vs HFRS differentiation, aiding clinical triage and surveillance. Limitations: Single‑center, abstract‑only data; external validation and recalibration are needed before clinical use.

papers.title_zh: 入院时临床实验室表型用于早期区分重症发热伴血小板减少综合征与 肾综合征出血热

analysis_zh.background: 在流行地区,早期区分重症发热伴血小板减少综合征(SFTS)和 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)仍然困难 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 一项单中心回顾性对比研究分析了2023年5月至2025年11月入院的330例经实验室确认的SFTS(n=220)或肾综合征出血热(HFRS,n=110)患者的入院时人口学、临床和实验室数据(A2);在完整案例数据集上构建了两套区分模型,并通过全流程嵌套交叉验证进行内部评估(A5)。
analysis_zh.results: SFTS患者年龄更大,女性比例更高,且表现出更多神经系统和血液学异常;而肾综合征出血热患者则出现更多泌尿、炎症和肾脏异常(A3);器官域负担分析证实了这些表型分离(A4)。基本模型和扩展模型的折叠外AUC分别为0.975和0.971,配对差异为–0.004(95% CI –0.014至0.005)(A6、A7);加入CRP、白蛋白和LDH并未始终提升预测性能(A8)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究提供了表型框架和高性能概念验证模型,用于早期区分SFTS与肾综合征出血热(HFRS),为临床分诊和监测提供依据(A4、A5、A9)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 研究结果来源于单中心,基于仅有的摘要数据,需在临床应用前进行独立的外部验证和重新校准(A9)。
